author: Gregory Thaumaturgus
occasion: A collection of brief moral and theological maxims, apparently preserved as excerpts, urging piety as the foundation of the virtues and contrasting sincere faith with costly but empty religion.
argument: The work opens by insisting that piety must be cultivated above all things, since it is rightly called the mother of the virtues and is their beginning and end. Knowledge of God as the sustaining and creating cause of all things is taught both by sight and by the natural law. The remaining sentences contrast simple, open-air faith with costly piety, and three gathered in the Lord's name with many who deny the Godhead. They affirm that a purified word and a soul perfected by the doctrines of truth are what is most magnificent to God, and that piety alone is an unchangeable and abiding good. Finally, they warn that what is not attainable is somehow not believed because of envy, since to profane souls nothing of good things is credible.

outline.move: Piety is to be cultivated above all as the mother, beginning, and end of the virtues, and knowledge of God as the sustaining and creating cause is taught by sight and the natural law.
Open-air faith is better than costly piety, and three gathered in the Lord's name are better than many denying the Godhead.
Nothing is so magnificent to God as a purified word and a soul perfected by the doctrines of truth, and piety alone is an unchangeable and abiding good.
What is not attainable is somehow not believed because of envy; for to profane souls nothing of good things is credible.

scripture: The source contains no explicit biblical citations, but the phrase 'three gathered in the name of the Lord' alludes to Matthew 18:20. If cited, use modern English Bible conventions.
uncertain: The original extent and structure of the work are unknown; only brief excerpts survive.
The date of composition cannot be established from the surviving text.
